newsitem.title: USA: US administration hails key Superfund lawsuit win.
newsitem.headline: US administration hails key Superfund lawsuit win.

text.p: The Clinton administration Thursday hailed a court ruling that endorsed its position that polluters, not taxpayers, should pay to clean up toxic waste they dumped in the past.

The case had been closely watched because Republicans and insurers have been pushing unsuccessfully to change the Superfund toxic waste cleanup law to make the government pick up the tab for billions of dollars in cleanup costs.

"The Court ruled that Superfund is constitutional and that polluters can be held responsible for the waste they dumped before 1980," said Assistant Attorney General Lois Schiffer, who argued the government's side in the case.
"With this ruling we can continue our commitment to faster, fairer and more efficient cleanups in every area of the country," she said in a statement.

The U.S. Court of Appeals 11th Circuit Tuesday reversed a lower court decision that would have let chemical manufacturer Olin Corp off the hook for paying to clean up toxic waste it had left on its property in McIntosh, Alabama.

Three appeals court judges in Atlanta unanimously rejected Olin's argument that the Superfund law could not be used to make companies clean sites where they had dumped waste legally before the Superfund law was passed, and where environmental damage was only on the company's property.

Olin officials were not immediately availabe to say whether they plan to appeal the decision to the Supreme Court. But insurance industry officials said an appeal was unlikely because the Atlanta court's decision was unanimous and in line with a string of previous court decisions.

"It would have changed the playing field (on Superfund) had it gone the other way," said John Arlington, senior counsel for the American Insurance Association. "It's a reminder that we've got to do something legislatively."
Chemical manufacturers have said they believe the best way for them to ease Superfund requirements would be to change the law in Congress instead of seeking relief in the courts.
